Insight: Baskets are not thin on average; outfits are incomplete. Among visits that include a garment, fewer than half (45%) are complete (top + bottom, or full-body).
Evidence (figure / number): Fig 5. Single-unit visits 30.1% (95% CI 30.0%-30.3%); mean 3.5 units per visit; garment visits: complete 45%, top only 38%, bottom only 17%.
So-what for the decision: The charter's 'buys one item and leaves' premise does not hold for the average shopper. Target the mirror at the top-only and bottom-only moments and set the items-per-bill baseline at about 3.5 units, not 1. Revise the uplift assumptions in the M6 simulation.
Confidence: High (H&M data); Medium for transfer to Westside

Insight: Thin baskets sit in one sales channel.
Evidence (figure / number): Section 7.1. Single-unit share 38% in channel 1 vs 25% in channel 2; units per visit about 2.5 vs 4.1.
So-what for the decision: If channel 1 is the physical store (the file does not say), the headroom is where the mirror will stand. Confirm the channel meaning before the simulation uses it; until then do not claim an in-store effect.

Insight: A customer's own history is a strong predictor only at the level of the exact article. Product type and colour history add little over what is popular that week.
Evidence (figure / number): Fig 6. Exact-article repeat 5.4% vs 0.3% random (19x); product type 1.26x; colour 1.07x; department 1.05x. 2,360,065 items evaluated.
So-what for the decision: Expect the recommender's edge over best-sellers to come from re-buy and from item-to-item cross-selling, not from learning a shopper's 'taste' in category or colour. Build article-level repeat and recency features first; treat taste embeddings as a second step.
Confidence: Medium (ratio depends on history length; measured on H&M only)

Insight: Purchases show which types are bought together, but not which are complements. Top x bottom pairs and top x top pairs have the same lift.
Evidence (figure / number): Fig 7. Median adjusted lift: top x bottom 1.35 (68% of pairs at 1.2 or more), top x top 1.36. Strongest top x bottom pair with 200+ visits: Vest top + Shorts (lift 1.82).
So-what for the decision: Use co-purchase only as a candidate generator for the outfit matcher. Compatibility must be learned from Polyvore outfit labels and judged on fill-in-the-blank accuracy, as the charter plans; do not evaluate the matcher on H&M co-purchase.

Insight: Demand turns over fast. A best-seller list is stale within weeks, and new articles carry a large share of sales.
Evidence (figure / number): Fig 9. Last week's top 12 / 100 / 500 cover 1.6% / 8.4% / 24.6% of next week's units. Top-100 overlap 0.29 at 1 week (sampling ceiling 0.37), 0.13 at 4 weeks, 0.05 at 52. 39% of weekly units come from articles first sold 8 weeks earlier or less.
So-what for the decision: Recompute the best-seller baseline weekly on a short window and validate by date, never by random rows. Forecasts and suggestions need an attribute-based fallback for new articles. The MAP@12 target of three times the baseline is demanding because the baseline itself is weak at the article level.

Insight: A minority of heavy buyers dominates the data and a large group has almost no history.
Evidence (figure / number): Fig 3. Top 10% of customers buy 48% of units (Gini 0.64); 32% of customers have one visit; customers with unknown age or club status have a median of 1 visit vs 3 for others.
So-what for the decision: Split train/test by customer, report metrics by activity tier, and weight or stratify so heavy buyers do not set the model. A third of members would meet the mirror with no history, so a popularity or content-based fallback is required, not optional.

Insight: Segments differ more in basket thinness than in what they buy. Older shoppers buy the fewest items per visit.
Evidence (figure / number): Fig 10. Single-unit share: 65+ 43% (CI 42%-45%), 18-24 34%, 25-34 27%; gap 17 points. Department mix vs age: Cramer's V 0.06 (weak).
So-what for the decision: Evaluate quality by age band at one fixed setting (M5 fairness plan). A pooled model will be tuned to 25-34 baskets; older shoppers need single-item completion. Department is only a weak age signal, so age cannot be inferred from what is in the basket.

Insight: Colour choice is concentrated in three neutrals and follows the season.
Evidence (figure / number): Fig 11. Black, White, Blue = 62% of units with a known colour. Light/bright share 42% in Jun-Aug vs 30% in Dec-Feb.
So-what for the decision: For about two thirds of purchases colour matching is a choice among neutrals, so the incremental value of skin-tone-based colour advice is likely small and must be shown in the M5 colour-choice comparison. Add month and season to every model.
Confidence: Medium (colour attribute is the catalogue's, not the shopper's)

Insight: The sample is not the bias; the proxy and the period are. The 10% sample matches the full file on every check, but 2020 is a structural break.
Evidence (figure / number): Figs 1-3. 6 of 6 representativeness checks pass on raw data and the cleaned frame (max |SMD| 0.02). Mar-Aug 2020 units were -13% vs 2019; channel-2 share 70% to 75%. Baby/Children is 3.8% of raw units and was removed.
So-what for the decision: Do not tune on the 2020 weeks alone; test models before and after March 2020. State in D4/D5 that results are patterns from European H&M data and must be re-validated on Westside data, as the charter says.

Insight: The 'single-item habit' group the charter targets is visible but small, and transactions cannot show confidence or effort.
Evidence (figure / number): Fig 12. Proxy (4+ visits, 60%+ single-unit): 9.7% of 61,014 repeat customers and 3.5% of their units; median 7 distinct product types vs 12.
So-what for the decision: Do not size the business case on this proxy. The shopper survey planned for M3 must establish whether low-effort, low-confidence dressers exist at Westside and how large the group is.
